naifu.meaning_mnemonic: A doomsday preacher holds up a sign reading the end is <reading>nigh</reading> in one hand and a whittled 「<reading>ナイフ</reading>」 in the other, the <vocabulary>knife</vocabulary> he used to cut the sign loose.

naka.meaning_mnemonic: Written alone, the <kanji>inside</kanji> kanji is simply the word for <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>.
naka.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's biggest shrine bell has a cat asleep <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary> it. <reading>Knock a</reading> bell like that and the yowl rings out from dead centre: <reading>なか</reading>.

naku.meaning_mnemonic: Water wells up along your lower lids until it spills over and runs down in two warm lines, and your breath keeps catching in hiccups. All of that at once is what it means to <vocabulary>cry</vocabulary>.
naku.reading_mnemonic: A kitten at the shrine keeps butting its head on the base of the huge bell, wanting up, and the soft <reading>knock</reading> of skull on bronze gets no answer. So it sits back and begins to <vocabulary>cry</vocabulary>, a thin 「<reading>なく</reading>」 going round the mossy steps.

nakunaru.meaning_mnemonic: You reach for the sugar and find the jar emptied to <kanji>nothingness</kanji> on its own. When the last of a thing quietly hits zero, it has <vocabulary>run out</vocabulary>.
nakunaru.reading_mnemonic: You already learned this reading of 無 from 無くす, so a thing fading out of the world by itself, <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary>, is <reading>なくなる</reading>.

nakusu.meaning_mnemonic: Your keys should be in the front pocket, but your fingers close on <kanji>nothingness</kanji>. When a thing drops out of the world like that, you <vocabulary>lose</vocabulary> it.
nakusu.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a goat headbutts your <reading>knapsack</reading> clean off the ledge, and you watch it shrink to a dot far below. To <vocabulary>lose</vocabulary> the lot in one shove like that is <reading>なくす</reading>.

namae.meaning_mnemonic: The evening hides your face, so your <kanji>name</kanji> is the one word you send out in <kanji>front</kanji> of you. A word carried ahead like that, so strangers know who just spoke, is your <vocabulary>name</vocabulary>.

nan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji still needs no help here. This reading just carries it forward as <vocabulary>what (before counters)</vocabulary>.
nan.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a hiker counts servings of <reading>naan</reading> bread. Before every number he blurts <reading>なん</reading>, as if <vocabulary>what (before counters)</vocabulary> always comes first.
nan.description: なん appears only right before a counter, as in questions about quantity or time. Used alone, 何 takes a different reading instead.

nana-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
nana-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a regular named <reading>Nana</reading> orders <vocabulary>seven</vocabulary> onigiri every visit, counting each one aloud as <reading>なな</reading>.

nanatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing. The trailing つ just turns the bare number into a count of objects.
nanatsu.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 七 is read なな, so <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>ななつ</reading>.

nani.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji needs no help to become a word. Alone, it already means <vocabulary>what</vocabulary>.
nani.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>nanny</reading> at Koichi's konbini opens a mystery tin and blurts <reading>なに</reading>. She still can't name <vocabulary>what</vocabulary> is inside.

nannji.meaning_mnemonic: Put <kanji>what</kanji> directly in front of <kanji>time</kanji> and you get the question itself, <vocabulary>what time</vocabulary>.

nanoka.meaning_mnemonic: String <kanji>seven</kanji> <kanji>suns</kanji> together and you get <vocabulary>seven days</vocabulary>, a full week gone by.

naosu.meaning_mnemonic: You could pretend the wobbly stool is fine, but <kanji>honesty</kanji> makes you admit the leg is loose, so you set it straight again. Owning what is broken and putting it right is what it means <vocabulary>to fix / repair</vocabulary> it.
naosu.reading_mnemonic: A customer sets a dead clock on the counter and says <reading>now, Sue</reading>. Sue always says yes, and handing a broken thing over to be set right is 「<reading>なおす</reading>」, <vocabulary>to fix / repair</vocabulary>.

naraberu.meaning_mnemonic: Take a shelf of jumbled cans and turn every label to face front, one behind the next, until they make a clean <kanji>row</kanji>. Setting objects out in a straight rank like that, by hand, is what it means <vocabulary>to line them up</vocabulary>.
naraberu.reading_mnemonic: A bell-ringer sets out her <reading>narrow bells</reading> along the rail, smallest to largest, so her hand can fall on each in turn. Putting things into one neat order along a line is 「<reading>ならべる</reading>」, <vocabulary>to line them up</vocabulary>.

naru-become.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a smooth green sapling out on the mountain trail for thirty years. Nobody prunes it, yet the trunk twists and <reading>gnarls</reading> on its own, and turning into something new like that is to <vocabulary>become</vocabulary> — <reading>なる</reading>.

naru-ring.meaning_mnemonic: A phone left face-down on the konbini counter lets out its full-volume <kanji>cry</kanji> with nobody near it. A thing sounding off by itself is what it means to <vocabulary>ring</vocabulary>.
naru-ring.reading_mnemonic: A shrine cat picks its way along a <reading>narrow</reading> beam, bumps the great hanging bell, and it goes 「<reading>なる</reading>」 right across the yard, the clear tone left ringing being a bell starting to <vocabulary>sound</vocabulary>.

naru.meaning_mnemonic: You sit beside someone who can already do the thing and copy them move for move until your hands pick the skill up on their own. Taking it straight off another person that way is what it means to <vocabulary>learn (from)</vocabulary> them.
naru.reading_mnemonic: A tame deer in <reading>Nara</reading> trails a calligraphy student all afternoon, scratching a copy of every stroke he makes into the dust. He watches it ape him and mutters 「<reading>ならう</reading>」, which is what it means to <vocabulary>learn (from)</vocabulary> someone.

natsu.meaning_mnemonic: By breakfast your shirt is stuck to your back and the ice in your glass is gone in a minute. When the sun is still glaring at eight at night, it is <vocabulary>summer</vocabulary>.
natsu.reading_mnemonic: At dusk on the riverbank a thick cloud of <reading>gnats</reading> finds the one lamp, and every walker passing under it mutters 「<reading>なつ</reading>」. The wet heat that hatched the whole swarm is <vocabulary>summer</vocabulary>.

naze.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, one kid stops every teacher to ask なぜ about the rules. He won't take one more step until he knows <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>.

nedan.meaning_mnemonic: Every item on the shelf is standing on one <kanji>step</kanji> of a tall staircase, and how far up its step sits is the thing's <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

neko.meaning_mnemonic: It shoves a glass off the table, watches it drop, holds your eye the whole time, then strolls away. That animal is a <vocabulary>cat</vocabulary>.
neko.reading_mnemonic: A visitor at Grandma Kane's shrine feels a warm weight land on her shoulders and a voice purr 「<reading>ねこ</reading>」 by her ear, like <reading>neck, oh</reading>. The thing draped over her collar is a <vocabulary>cat</vocabulary>.

nen-year.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>year</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>year (counter)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they mean the same thing.

neru.meaning_mnemonic: Your eyes slam shut and the book drops onto your face. The whole day switches off by itself, and you <vocabulary>sleep</vocabulary>.
neru.reading_mnemonic: A student with no <reading>nerve</reading> left flops face down onto the desk. The second the hallway goes quiet, he starts to <vocabulary>sleep</vocabulary>, letting out a slow 「<reading>ねる</reading>」.

ni-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>two</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.

nichi-day.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>day</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>day (counter)</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean the same thing.

nichiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> is too bright to share the sky, so the very first <kanji>weekday</kanji> takes its name straight from it, becoming <vocabulary>Sunday</vocabulary>.

nigiyaka.meaning_mnemonic: On sports day the school field runs three races at once, a brass band, and parents yelling from every rail. All that noise and motion piled together is <vocabulary>lively / bustling</vocabulary>.
nigiyaka.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank festival, the most packed, roaring stall belongs to a fishmonger called <reading>Knee-gear-yakker</reading>. That wall of noise and elbows is <vocabulary>lively / bustling</vocabulary>, the very sound of <reading>にぎやか</reading>.

nihon.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> clears the horizon here first, at the very <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. That country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.
nihon.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the top of the mountain trail watches the sunrise and raps her <reading>knee bone</reading> twice for the beats as she names the country it rises over, 「<reading>にほん</reading>」, and that country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.

nihongo.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> rises first over the land at the <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. The <kanji>language</kanji> they speak there is <vocabulary>Japanese</vocabulary>.
nihongo.reading_mnemonic: The school's race starter lost her whistle, so she now starts every heat by barking the one scrap of <vocabulary>Japanese</vocabulary> she knows, '<reading>knee-honk-go</reading>,' and the runners hear it as 「<reading>にほんご</reading>」.

niku.meaning_mnemonic: Overnight, every shelf in Koichi's konbini is restocked with nothing but <vocabulary>meat</vocabulary>. Cold steaks fill the onigiri rack, sausages crowd the drinks fridge, and a slab of ribs beeps through the till.

nimotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Any <kanji>thing</kanji> you own that isn't nailed down, crammed into two bags for the trip, becomes your <vocabulary>luggage</vocabulary>.

nin-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Stand in a doorway and tap each <kanji>person</kanji> on the shoulder as they stride through on the two legs you already know. Every tap adds one more to your count of <vocabulary>people (counter)</vocabulary>.

nishi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>west</kanji> kanji is the entire <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> word by itself, so the two mean precisely the same thing.
nishi-v.reading_mnemonic: Every evening the sinking sun burns a glowing <reading>niche</reading> into the <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> wall of the shrine. The cats curl into that <reading>にし</reading>-shaped alcove for the last of the warmth.

niwa.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the strip of bare ground that a Japanese house wraps itself around, half swept dirt and half stubborn weeds. The family still points at that patch and proudly calls it the <vocabulary>garden / yard</vocabulary>.
niwa.reading_mnemonic: Every time Nao kneels in the mossy patch behind Grandma Kane's shrine, a resident cat leans in and yowls one long <reading>nee-wah</reading>. That is how <reading>にわ</reading> got stuck to the <vocabulary>garden / yard</vocabulary> she was weeding.

noboru.meaning_mnemonic: The only way up to the tree house is the knotted rope, hand over hand, feet slipping on bark. Hauling yourself up something steep like that, using your whole body, is what it means <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary>.
noboru.reading_mnemonic: That is a goat on the barn roof, <reading>no bull</reading> about it, picking its way straight up the near-vertical face. Working slowly up something that steep is 「<reading>のぼる</reading>」, <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary>.

nokoru.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone clears out of the classroom at the bell. The one bag still by the window, after the rest are gone, is what <vocabulary>remains</vocabulary>.
nokoru.reading_mnemonic: The tide pulls every shell off the rocks but one clinging starfish, and a kid yells <reading>no, Coral</reading> at it, 「<reading>のこる</reading>」, and that lone holdout after the rest are gone is what <vocabulary>remains</vocabulary>.

nomimono.meaning_mnemonic: Among all the nameless <kanji>things</kanji> in the barn, the one you tip up and <kanji>drink</kanji> instead of chewing is the <vocabulary>drink</vocabulary>.

nomu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>drink</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to drink</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning does not shift. The tail kana only turns it into the verb you aim at a full glass of water.
nomu-v.reading_mnemonic: A sun-baked desert <reading>nomad</reading> reaches the well and tips the whole bucket back. He will not stop until it runs dry, then sighs 「<reading>のむ</reading>」 with nothing left to <vocabulary>drink</vocabulary>.

nooto.meaning_mnemonic: You scribble one <reading>note</reading>, then a hundred more, then clamp the whole pile flat between two cardboard covers. That fat brick of paper is a 「<reading>ノート</reading>」, your <vocabulary>notebook</vocabulary>.

noru.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a peaked cap hauls itself up into the night bus and grabs the rail as the bus pulls away. That scramble up onto a moving vehicle is what it means to <vocabulary>board</vocabulary>.
noru.reading_mnemonic: The badger's electric bus rolls up with <reading>no roar</reading> at all, so you almost miss it in the dark. Jump on before the doors close and you 「<reading>のる</reading>」 — you <vocabulary>ride</vocabulary>.

nugu.meaning_mnemonic: The only way to <kanji>escape</kanji> a soaked raincoat is to peel it down off your arms and let it drop. Peeling a garment off your body like that is what it means to <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary>.
nugu.reading_mnemonic: A walrus flops onto the riverbank and drags its dripping wetsuit off over its head. It grunts 「<reading>ぬぐ</reading>」 as a cold <reading>nugget</reading> of riverweed plops from the sleeve, because it will <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary> anywhere.

oba.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mother</kanji> figure who's still just a <kanji>youth</kanji> herself, holding kids anyway, is your <vocabulary>aunt</vocabulary>.
oba.reading_mnemonic: Your aunt hikes to the mountain trail's summit just to blast one horrible note on an oboe, and that screech is <reading>おば</reading> — <reading>"oboe"</reading> — the sound of your <vocabulary>aunt</vocabulary> announcing her arrival.
oba.description: An aunt younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

obaasan.meaning_mnemonic: An old woman dozes in a sunbeam and lets out a long, satisfied <reading>おばあさん</reading> — <reading>"ohh, baa, sun"</reading> — and that sigh is exactly what you call your <vocabulary>grandmother (polite)</vocabulary>.
obaasan.description: Also used to politely address any elderly woman, not just your own grandmother.

oboeru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>memorize</vocabulary> a list is just <kanji>remembering</kanji> forced on purpose. You drill each item into your skull, over and over, until it cannot slip back out.
oboeru.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing school hallway a kid plays the same four bars on her <reading>oboe</reading>, eyes shut, until her fingers move on their own. Drilling something in until it sticks like that is <reading>おぼえる</reading>, which is how you <vocabulary>memorize</vocabulary> anything.

ocha.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tea</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>tea</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing; meeting it again as a word changes nothing.
ocha.description: In everyday Japanese お茶 usually means green tea, not tea in general.

ochiru.meaning_mnemonic: A ripe chestnut lets go of its branch above the mountain trail. It <vocabulary>falls</vocabulary> to the path on its own, with no hand anywhere near it.
ochiru.reading_mnemonic: A clumsy window-cleaner loses his grip on the ledge, gives the street a cheery <reading>oh, cheerio</reading>, and goes 「<reading>おちる</reading>」 straight down past every floor, a plain helpless <vocabulary>fall</vocabulary>.

odoru.meaning_mnemonic: Your hips swing, your feet cross and stamp, and your arms cut shapes in the air in time with a beat. All that patterned motion to music is what it means to <vocabulary>dance</vocabulary>.
odoru.reading_mnemonic: By the mountain vending machine a hiker feeds in coins, gets nothing back, and starts kicking and spinning at the little coin-return <reading>door</reading> in a rage. From a distance the flailing looks like he chose to <vocabulary>dance</vocabulary>, stamping 「<reading>おどる</reading>」 into the gravel.

ohayou.meaning_mnemonic: Say the word slowly and it comes out as <reading>Ohio</reading>, the American state. Land that sound before dawn and you have <reading>おはよう</reading>, the <vocabulary>good morning</vocabulary> you give before anyone has had coffee.

oishii.meaning_mnemonic: You try the free sample at Koichi's konbini, your eyebrows shoot up, and all you can say is '<reading>oh, I see</reading>' — now you finally get the queue outside. That jolt of understanding is 「<reading>おいしい</reading>」, <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>, and its final い marks it as an adjective.

oji.meaning_mnemonic: A backup <kanji>father</kanji> who shows up every holiday, spoils you rotten, and sneaks you extra sweets is your <vocabulary>uncle</vocabulary>.
oji.reading_mnemonic: Your uncle trips over a shrine cat and yelps <reading>おじ</reading> — <reading>"oh, gee!"</reading> — the sound your <vocabulary>uncle</vocabulary> makes every single visit.
oji.description: An uncle younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

ojiisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a <vocabulary>grandfather (polite)</vocabulary> groans 「<reading>おじいさん</reading>」, sounding just like <reading>oh, geez, Sam</reading>, every time his grandson rings the giant bell too hard.

okaasan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji is already mother, so <vocabulary>mother (polite)</vocabulary> just wraps that same meaning in politeness.
okaasan.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, your <vocabulary>mother (polite)</vocabulary> pulls up in a squealing <reading>car</reading> right through the automatic doors. The cashier just sighs, '<reading>おかあさん</reading>, not again'.
okaasan.description: Use お母さん to speak to or about someone else's mother. For your own mother, switch to the plainer 母 when talking to an outsider.

okaerinasai.meaning_mnemonic: You hand the sweeper to whoever just <kanji>returned</kanji> through the front door, and the greeting that goes with it is <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary>.
okaerinasai.reading_mnemonic: You already know 帰 is 「かえ」 from 帰る, so <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary> is <reading>おかえりなさい</reading>.

okane.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>money</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>money</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
okane.reading_mnemonic: The collection box at Grandma Kane's shrine only fills when a visitor gasps '<reading>oh, Kane</reading>' and drops in a coin, so the cats now bolt for the <vocabulary>money</vocabulary> the instant they hear 「<reading>おかね</reading>」.

okashi.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Cakes</kanji> come in adult size, but shrink each one to <kanji>child</kanji> size and you can eat twelve without comment. A bowl of those miniatures is <vocabulary>sweets / snacks</vocabulary>.

okiru.meaning_mnemonic: The alarm has howled for a full hour. Your eyes crack open, your back peels off the futon, and you <vocabulary>wake up / get up</vocabulary>.
okiru.reading_mnemonic: Roo the kangaroo has fallen asleep on Koichi's onigiri shelf. Koichi shakes him and says <reading>OK, Roo</reading>, so the kangaroo finally has to <vocabulary>wake up / get up</vocabulary>, yawning <reading>おきる</reading>.

oku.meaning_mnemonic: You set the heavy box down on the floor exactly where you want it, then lift your hands away. Leaving a thing to rest in a chosen spot is to <vocabulary>put</vocabulary> it there.
oku.reading_mnemonic: A hiker lugs a stool carved from <reading>oak</reading> up the mountain trail and stands it square beside the vending machine, 「<reading>おく</reading>」, and setting a thing down in one chosen spot is to <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> it.

okureru.meaning_mnemonic: The last train slides out of the station without you. Slipping behind the clock, with only your slow feet to blame, is to <vocabulary>be late</vocabulary>.
okureru.reading_mnemonic: Sei stops at the konbini for a bag of <reading>okra</reading> and strolls in after the bell, 「<reading>おくれる</reading>」, and turning up once the moment has passed is to <vocabulary>be late</vocabulary>.

okuru.meaning_mnemonic: A parcel bound for another city and a friend boarding the last train get the very same treatment: you hand it over, then stand there watching it get smaller. That watching-it-leave is what it means to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary>.
okuru.reading_mnemonic: Every week the farmer mails a crate of <reading>okra</reading> to her sister and weeps on the platform as the train goes. The town decided that to <reading>おくる</reading> is to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary> with your whole heart.

okusan.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever rules the <kanji>interior</kanji> of the house earns the title <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary>.
okusan.reading_mnemonic: Everyone in the village calls her <reading>おくさん</reading>. She stands as sturdy as an <reading>oak</reading>, so of course she is the <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary> of the house.

omoi.meaning_mnemonic: A suitcase you pack full of bricks and then cannot drag an inch across the floor is <vocabulary>heavy</vocabulary>. The い on the end is what makes it an adjective, the same ending every describing word like it takes.
omoi.reading_mnemonic: Old Omura hoists the crate at the riverbank, then feels his back give way. He groans <reading>oh my</reading>, because the crate is <reading>おもい</reading>, far too <vocabulary>heavy</vocabulary> to lift another inch.

omoshiroi.meaning_mnemonic: A clown's <kanji>mask</kanji>, painted flat <kanji>white</kanji>, is the thing the whole room turns to watch. Whatever pulls every eye in a room like that is <vocabulary>interesting / funny</vocabulary>.

omou.meaning_mnemonic: You never reason this kind out; you just hold it, the way you cup a warm mug or trust a quiet hunch. Carrying an opinion around like that is to <vocabulary>think, to feel</vocabulary>.
omou.reading_mnemonic: A cow in the evening field watches the sunset and lets out a slow, thoughtful <reading>oh, moo</reading>. No reasoning behind it, only a feeling about the day, and that quiet sense of <vocabulary>thinking, of feeling</vocabulary> a thing is <reading>おもう</reading>.

onaji.meaning_mnemonic: Two socks from one dryer load, worn to a matching grey heel, are for every purpose the <vocabulary>same</vocabulary>. Handle it as a な adjective, so な lands before the noun it describes.
onaji.reading_mnemonic: At roll call the teacher finds three girls all named after one gran and just sighs <reading>oh, Nan, gee</reading>. She logs them as a single entry, because the girls really are the <vocabulary>same</vocabulary>, and that sigh is <reading>おなじ</reading>.

onaka.meaning_mnemonic: The soft drum you pat after a big lunch, the part that growls in a silent room, is your <vocabulary>stomach / belly</vocabulary>.
onaka.reading_mnemonic: One more dumpling drifts toward the sumo trainee and he waves it off, both palms flat on his <vocabulary>stomach / belly</vocabulary>: <reading>oh, not a</reading>nother bite. The groan lands as 「<reading>おなか</reading>」.

oneesan.meaning_mnemonic: A lost traveler at the riverbank asks a young woman for directions, calling her <vocabulary>older sister (polite)</vocabulary> before he even learns her name.
oneesan.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the new clerk stretches her greeting into a horse-like 「<reading>おねえさん</reading>」, drawing out the <reading>neigh</reading> so long that customers laugh. They still call her an <vocabulary>older sister (polite)</vocabulary> right back.
oneesan.description: Use お姉さん for any young woman addressed politely — a shop clerk, a stranger — not only an actual older sister.

onegaishimasu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>request</kanji> held out flat in both hands, with <vocabulary>please</vocabulary> set on top like a bow on a box. That polite wrapping around the ask is the whole word.
onegaishimasu.reading_mnemonic: You hold the door for a courier whose arms are stacked with boxes and call <reading>おねがいします</reading>, which lands like <reading>oh, need I ask</reading>. You hardly do, so the word is a light, polite <vocabulary>please</vocabulary>.

ongaku.meaning_mnemonic: Take the kind of <kanji>sound</kanji> that makes you sit up in a silent room and string it along a branch like ice beads until sitting and listening is pure <kanji>comfort</kanji>. That is <vocabulary>music</vocabulary>.

ongakushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Pack every <kanji>sound</kanji> a school makes into one room where the only <kanji>music</kanji> is on the timetable, and that is the <vocabulary>music room</vocabulary>.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: A tired customer at Koichi's konbini calls the teenage clerk an <vocabulary>older brother (polite)</vocabulary> before he even rings up her onigiri, though they have never met.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker clutches his aching <reading>knee</reading> and yells 「<reading>おにいさん</reading>」, begging the <vocabulary>older brother (polite)</vocabulary> leading the group to slow down.
oniisan.description: Use お兄さん for any young man addressed politely — a waiter, a stranger — not only an actual older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: The door meant for any <kanji>person</kanji> gets repainted with a <kanji>woman</kanji> stick figure, so now it specifies exactly which <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary> may enter.
onnanohito.description: 女 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific woman; 女の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: A costume shop sells a miniature <kanji>woman</kanji> outfit sized only for a <kanji>child</kanji>, and whoever fits into it is simply called a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>.

ookii.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>big</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> word are the same character. The kana tail ending in い is the part that makes it an adjective, and every い adjective after this works the same way.
ookii.reading_mnemonic: A mover tilts a wardrobe off the truck and finds it is too <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> to fit through the front gate. He stands there stuck, muttering <reading>oh, oh, key</reading> — <reading>おおきい</reading>.

oriru.meaning_mnemonic: The chairlift on the mountain trail carries you up, and where the cable turns you <kanji>descend</kanji> from the seat onto the snow. That hop down off the lift is how you <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary>.
oriru.reading_mnemonic: Ori the lift attendant sighs <reading>'oh, really'</reading> at every skier who freezes on the unloading ramp. Only when they hear his flat 「<reading>おりる</reading>」 do they finally <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary> the chair.

orosu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>down</kanji> kanji sits right inside <vocabulary>to lower</vocabulary>, the same downward move. The trailing kana add a pair of hands, so you take hold of a real object and bring it down yourself.
orosu.reading_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini a crate of frozen <reading>walrus</reading> steaks sits jammed on the top shelf. He wraps both arms around it and works it down to the floor, with a grunt of 「<reading>おろす</reading>」 at every step, until he has <vocabulary>lowered</vocabulary> the whole load.

osake.meaning_mnemonic: Leave cooked rice and clean river water together in a warm, dark cupboard for a few weeks. The mixture quietly ferments into <vocabulary>alcohol / sake</vocabulary>.
osake.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's neighbour <reading>O'Sakey</reading> climbs the mossy steps each evening with one bottle and nothing else. Two cups of <reading>おさけ</reading> later he is asleep among the cats, and the name has stuck to the <vocabulary>alcohol / sake</vocabulary> in his hand.

oshieru.meaning_mnemonic: You take something you know cold and load it, piece by piece, into a head that did not have it an hour ago. Doing that on purpose, until it sticks in the other person, is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.
oshieru.reading_mnemonic: A new student in the echoing hallway watches the tutor break every hard idea into clean steps and thinks, <reading>oh, she rules</reading>. The tutor smiles and says 「<reading>おしえる</reading>」, and handing knowledge over like that is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.

osoi.meaning_mnemonic: You order a hot coffee at Koichi's konbini and it arrives the following Tuesday, cold, with a note apologising. Nobody waits a week for coffee unless the service is <vocabulary>slow / late</vocabulary>.
osoi.reading_mnemonic: A snail on the school field is <reading>oh so</reading> relaxed that the nets come down before it reaches the centre line. By the time it crosses, the field is dark and empty, which is exactly <reading>おそい</reading>, or <vocabulary>slow / late</vocabulary>.

otearai.meaning_mnemonic: The room set aside for you to <kanji>wash</kanji> your <kanji>hand</kanji> in is the one polite people call the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>.

otokonohito.meaning_mnemonic: Someone asks who that <kanji>person</kanji> is, still out in the field flexing all that power. It's simply the <kanji>man</kanji> you already know, nothing more than a <vocabulary>man</vocabulary>.
otokonohito.description: 男 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific man; 男の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

otokonoko.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>man</kanji> in the rice field has a <kanji>child</kanji> copying him, flexing a tiny arm, too small to plow anything. That miniature power alone is what makes a <vocabulary>boy</vocabulary>.

otona.meaning_mnemonic: Once a <kanji>person</kanji> gets <kanji>big</kanji> enough, everyone starts calling them an <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary>.
otona.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, only an <reading>おとな</reading> may ring the great bell, so the cats call the rule keeper <reading>Otto Nana</reading>, guardian of every <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary> visitor.
otona.description: As a な adjective, it takes な directly before the noun it describes, not い like most descriptive words.

otosu.meaning_mnemonic: You fumble your phone above the konbini counter and your fingers open. A hand let it go, so when you <vocabulary>drop</vocabulary> a thing, the fault is yours.
otosu.reading_mnemonic: You met this reading of 落 back in 落ちる, so when a hand is what lets the thing go, <vocabulary>to drop</vocabulary> it is <reading>おとす</reading>.

ototoi.meaning_mnemonic: Count back <kanji>one</kanji> more <kanji>day</kanji> past yesterday and you land on <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary>.
ototoi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank an <reading>otter toy</reading> washes ashore two days late, stamped <reading>おととい</reading> for <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary> it went missing.

otousan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>father</kanji> kanji already means father, and <vocabulary>father (polite)</vocabulary> is simply the respectful way to say that very same word.
otousan.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail, your <reading>おとうさん</reading> keeps <reading>towing</reading> your backpack up the last steep stretch. That's just what a <vocabulary>father (polite)</vocabulary> does for you.
otousan.description: Use お父さん to speak to or about someone else's father. For your own father, switch to the plainer 父 when talking to an outsider.

otouto.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the smallest hiker races ahead of everyone and falls straight into the vending machine at the top. That reckless little kid is exactly a <vocabulary>younger brother</vocabulary>.
otouto.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team's littlest <vocabulary>younger brother</vocabulary> mascot revs an invisible <reading>auto</reading> down the hallway, yelling 「<reading>おとうと</reading>」 every time he nearly crashes.

otsuri.meaning_mnemonic: Pay with a note that is far too big and the cashier lets you <kanji>angle</kanji> a fistful of coins back out of the deal. That catch is your <vocabulary>change (money)</vocabulary>.
otsuri.reading_mnemonic: Koichi at the konbini takes your big note and pushes a heap of coins back across the beeping till. You walk out not <reading>utterly</reading> broke, that heap in your palm being your <vocabulary>change (money)</vocabulary>, 「<reading>おつり</reading>」.

otto.meaning_mnemonic: The one who groans the loudest fixing a leaky faucet at 2 AM is your <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>.
otto.reading_mnemonic: He trips over the cat and yelps <reading>おっと</reading> every morning. It sounds exactly like <reading>oops</reading>, and that's exactly why he's the <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>.

owari.meaning_mnemonic: The last stop on the mountain trail, past the vending machine, where the path simply quits, is the <vocabulary>end</vocabulary>.
owari.reading_mnemonic: You already know that sound from 終わる, so the noun for where things stop, <vocabulary>end</vocabulary>, is <reading>おわり</reading>.

owaru.meaning_mnemonic: Follow a road all the way to its <kanji>end</kanji> and there is no more road left to walk. Something that runs itself out like that, with nobody stopping it, is <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.
owaru.reading_mnemonic: A walrus down at the riverbank waits for the very last of the light, then flops onto the final rock with nothing left to do. Say <reading>oh, walrus</reading> and you land on <reading>おわる</reading>, the day come <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.

oyasuminasai.meaning_mnemonic: At lights-out Sei mumbles <reading>おやすみなさい</reading> into the pillow, a slurred <reading>oh-yah-soo-me-nah-sigh</reading> that trails off into a yawn. It is the <vocabulary>good night</vocabulary> you say heading to sleep, not the one you say leaving a room.

oyogu.meaning_mnemonic: A dog dropped into the river flattens out, paddles hard with all four legs, and pushes itself forward across the water. It has started to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>.
oyogu.reading_mnemonic: A farmer tips a vat of yogurt down his front at the riverbank and wades in to rinse off. The current grabs him, and now he has to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>, spitting out <reading>oh, yogurt</reading>, which comes out as <reading>およぐ</reading>.

pan.meaning_mnemonic: A baker too cheap to buy an oven fries every loaf of <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary> in one battered <reading>pan</reading>. Ask him what it is and he just grunts <reading>パン</reading>.

pasokon.meaning_mnemonic: You tap your <reading>passcode in</reading> and the grey slab wakes up with a low hum. That machine, dead weight until you prove who you are and then able to run your whole day, is the <vocabulary>computer</vocabulary> everyone calls the <reading>パソコン</reading>.

pen.meaning_mnemonic: Stand two hundred <reading>ペン</reading> upright in the mud in a big rectangle and you have fenced off a pig <reading>pen</reading>. Every post in that fence is one <vocabulary>pen</vocabulary>.

raigetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The rice due to <kanji>come</kanji> up won't be ready until one more lap of the <kanji>moon</kanji> finishes, and that lap is <vocabulary>next month</vocabulary>.

rainen.meaning_mnemonic: Another chevron is about to <kanji>come</kanji>, scratched onto the shield-board for a <kanji>year</kanji> that hasn't happened yet: <vocabulary>next year</vocabulary>.

raishuu.meaning_mnemonic: A crop that hasn't <kanji>come</kanji> up yet breaks the surface on the <kanji>week</kanji> after this one, which is exactly <vocabulary>next week</vocabulary>.

rajio.meaning_mnemonic: The crackly play-by-play blaring over every <reading>rodeo</reading> comes out of one dented box wired to a fence post. All voices and no picture, that box is the <vocabulary>radio</vocabulary>, and the hands at the ring just call it the <reading>ラジオ</reading>.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the annual bell inspection turns up nothing wrong, and the inspector announces the crack count in his most formal voice: <vocabulary>zero (formal)</vocabulary>.
rei.description: 零 marks the formal, technical zero, used in temperatures, exam scores, and official readings, where everyday speech reaches for a plainer word instead.

reizouko.meaning_mnemonic: Keep a cupboard-sized <kanji>storehouse</kanji> <kanji>cool</kanji> around the clock, and that humming little <kanji>warehouse</kanji> in the corner of your kitchen is a <vocabulary>refrigerator</vocabulary>.

rekishi.meaning_mnemonic: Write down every <kanji>passage of time</kanji> a place has lived through, one year stacked on the last, and the finished pile is its <vocabulary>history</vocabulary>.

renshuu-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Running the same scale, the same kick, the same brush stroke over and over until your hands do it without you watching is what it means <vocabulary>to practice</vocabulary>.

resutoran.meaning_mnemonic: Chant it and <reading>「レストラン」</reading> falls apart into <reading>rest, oh, ran</reading>. That is you flopping down to rest because you just ran here starving, and the place that then feeds you is a <vocabulary>restaurant</vocabulary>.

riyuu.meaning_mnemonic: A toddler shoves a plant pot off the sill, meets your eyes, and plainly had a <vocabulary>reason</vocabulary>. You are never going to find out what it was.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing was ever added to the <kanji>six</kanji> kanji, so the <vocabulary>six</vocabulary> word is just that same kanji standing alone.

ryokan.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>building</kanji> that fills only with people partway through a <kanji>trip</kanji>, then empties again the morning they move on, is an <vocabulary>inn</vocabulary>.

ryokou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Shoulder your pack for a <kanji>trip</kanji> and keep choosing to <kanji>go</kanji> at every crossroads, one town after the next. Staying on the move like that, wherever the road forks, is what it is <vocabulary>to travel</vocabulary>.

ryokou.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>trip</kanji> stays a daydream until the two of you follow the banner to the crossroads and actually <kanji>go</kanji>. Once your feet move, that is <vocabulary>trip / travel</vocabulary>.

ryouri-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You take raw <kanji>materials</kanji> and run them through the strict <kanji>logic</kanji> of a recipe, step after step. When that turns them into a hot meal, you <vocabulary>cook</vocabulary>.

ryouri.meaning_mnemonic: Raw <kanji>materials</kanji> on the counter mean nothing until you add <kanji>logic</kanji> about heat, water and timing. That worked-out plan for the ingredients is <vocabulary>cooking</vocabulary>.

ryoushuusho.meaning_mnemonic: Your money crosses into the shop's <kanji>dominion</kanji>, and they <kanji>take it in</kanji> as payment now settled. The slip they <kanji>write</kanji> to prove that changed hands is your <vocabulary>receipt</vocabulary>.

sagaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>down</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary> verb are one and the same direction. With the trailing kana it becomes the verb for that drop happening by itself, with no hand on it.
sagaru.reading_mnemonic: High on the mountain trail a rain-soaked <reading>saguaro</reading> cactus can no longer hold up its arms. One heavy limb sags lower and lower on its own, with a dry rasp of 「<reading>さがる</reading>」, and that slow droop is what it means to <vocabulary>fall</vocabulary>.

sagasu.meaning_mnemonic: Your ring slips off at the riverbank and vanishes into the reeds, so now you are on your knees parting every stalk. Going over a place inch by inch after one lost thing is what it means <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> it.
sagasu.reading_mnemonic: A reader wants the old Norse <reading>sagas</reading>, and the librarian is up the ladder again, running one finger along the spines. Combing a whole wall of shelves for a single book is 「<reading>さがす</reading>」, <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> it.

sai-age.meaning_mnemonic: Every birthday you get through stacks one more ring of <kanji>age</kanji> onto the pile inside you. Count the rings in that stack and the number is how many <vocabulary>years old</vocabulary> you are.

saifu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Wealth</kanji> in your pocket is just loose paper and coins. Fold a scrap of <kanji>cloth</kanji> around it and the closed pouch is a <vocabulary>wallet</vocabulary>.

saigo.meaning_mnemonic: Let your <kanji>behind</kanji> foot drag as far back as a foot can possibly go, out to the <kanji>utmost</kanji> extreme. That trailing spot is the <vocabulary>last / end</vocabulary> of the line.

saisho.meaning_mnemonic: Shove your way to the <kanji>utmost</kanji> front of the queue, as far forward as a person can stand. That spot at the very head of everything is the <vocabulary>first / beginning</vocabulary>.

sakana.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fish</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>fish</vocabulary> word are the same, so they mean the same thing.
sakana.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, Ana wrings out a soaking wet <reading>sock</reading> and a live <vocabulary>fish</vocabulary> drops out of the heel. Ana's sock full of fish is <reading>さかな</reading>.

samui.meaning_mnemonic: The final い makes this an adjective, so you can pin it straight onto a noun. Picture a flat grey sky with your breath hanging in the air and the puddles frozen hard, and that whole outdoor chill is <vocabulary>cold (weather)</vocabulary>.
samui.reading_mnemonic: A courier named <reading>Sam</reading> restocks the mountain-trail vending machine at dawn, hopping and hugging himself. He groans about why it is always this <reading>さむい</reading>, and the frost-white empty trail around him is <vocabulary>cold (weather)</vocabulary> in one picture.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: There's no gap between the <kanji>three</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>three</vocabulary> word — write one and you've written the other.

sanpo-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Your feet stop flat every few steps and the path just <kanji>scatters</kanji> wherever it likes, aiming nowhere. A <kanji>walk</kanji> that loose and unplanned is you choosing to <vocabulary>take a walk</vocabulary>.

sara.meaning_mnemonic: A shallow ceramic circle you heap food onto and later scrape clean is a <vocabulary>plate / dish</vocabulary>.
sara.reading_mnemonic: At the buffet every <reading>salad</reading> is carried out on its own wide white 「<reading>さら</reading>」, the only <vocabulary>plate / dish</vocabulary> broad enough to hold it.

satou.meaning_mnemonic: Tip the bag and it hisses out like dry <kanji>sand</kanji>. A spoonful of that pale grit turns your coffee sweet, so it has to be <vocabulary>sugar</vocabulary>.

satsu-counter.meaning_mnemonic: You count anything bound between covers, from novels to textbooks to thin manga, by sliding them onto a shelf one spine at a time. The number of spines lined up in a row is how many <vocabulary>books</vocabulary> you have.

sayounara.meaning_mnemonic: Draw it out on the platform as the train pulls away, the way you would a slow <reading>so long</reading>. That heavy, drawn-out <reading>さようなら</reading> is the <vocabulary>goodbye</vocabulary> that means a good while.
sayounara.description: Heavier than the English 'bye'. It suggests a long separation, so to family or coworkers you will see tomorrow it can sound oddly final; day-to-day partings use lighter phrases.

seito.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>life</kanji> still in its <kanji>junior</kanji> stage, trailing a few steps behind the teacher, is a <vocabulary>pupil</vocabulary>.

seki-seat.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has one dry step among twenty wet ones. Whoever loses the dawn scramble for it loses their <vocabulary>seat</vocabulary>.

sekken.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>stone</kanji>-hard bar that gives up its <kanji>saltiness</kanji> as slippery lather the moment it meets water is <vocabulary>soap</vocabulary>.

semai.meaning_mnemonic: You meet someone in the shrine hallway and you both have to turn sideways to squeeze past, because the walls sit that close together. A passage like that is <vocabulary>narrow / cramped</vocabulary>, and the final い makes it an adjective.
semai.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>semi</reading> truck noses into the alley behind Koichi's konbini and stops dead, wedged tight between the two walls. The alley is <reading>せまい</reading>, far too <vocabulary>narrow / cramped</vocabulary> for a truck that size.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thousand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>thousand</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, doing double duty as itself.

sengetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The one already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of you finished its <kanji>moon</kanji>-lap before you did, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last month</vocabulary>.

sensei.meaning_mnemonic: Someone whose <kanji>life</kanji> is already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of yours on the path knows the way, which makes them your <vocabulary>teacher</vocabulary>.

senshuu.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever strode <kanji>ahead</kanji> already crossed the <kanji>week</kanji> before this one, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last week</vocabulary>.

sentaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>wash</kanji> here is not the dishes and not your hands, but a heaped basket of dirty shirts and socks. That one narrowed-down job is exactly what it means to <vocabulary>do laundry</vocabulary>.

setsumei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You hold your <kanji>theory</kanji> up and keep rephrasing it until it goes <kanji>bright</kanji> in the other person's head. Making it light up like that is how you <vocabulary>explain</vocabulary> it.

shashin.meaning_mnemonic: Freeze one moment as a <kanji>true</kanji> copy, exact enough that nobody can deny it happened. That undeniable copy of real life is a <vocabulary>photograph</vocabulary>.

shatsu.meaning_mnemonic: You button the cloth from collar to hem until it <reading>shuts</reading> flat against your chest. That sealed panel of fabric you tuck into your trousers is a <vocabulary>shirt</vocabulary>, the one you call 「<reading>シャツ</reading>」.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: Four (alt) is simply the <kanji>four</kanji> kanji on its own, so the kanji and the <vocabulary>four (alt)</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven (alt)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, meaning exactly what the kanji already taught you.

shigoto.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> you loyally <kanji>attend</kanji> to day after day, sandals fetched and tea poured, is your <vocabulary>work / job</vocabulary>.

shigotoba.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>place</kanji> you show up to each day to <kanji>attend</kanji> to the <kanji>business</kanji> that pays you, fetching and carrying until closing, is your <vocabulary>workplace</vocabulary>.

shikashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <reading>cashier</reading> rings up your jackpot ticket with a straight face, <reading>しかし</reading> the drawer slides open on nothing but paperclips. That hard turn from win to nothing is what <vocabulary>however</vocabulary> does to a sentence.

shiken.meaning_mnemonic: A single formal <kanji>try</kanji> that the school scores, records, and later holds against your name is an <vocabulary>exam</vocabulary>.

shimeru.meaning_mnemonic: When the last class leaves, the caretaker at Sei's school walks the hallway pulling every window down and easing every classroom door shut. Bringing something that stood open back to shut is <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary> it.
shimeru.reading_mnemonic: A hard white <reading>shimmer</reading> bounces off the gym windows and blinds every free throw at Sei's school. So the coach sends a player <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary> <reading>しめる</reading> the blinds before practice.

shinbun.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>newspaper</vocabulary> gathers everything <kanji>new</kanji> that people around town managed to <kanji>hear</kanji>. By morning the whole pile is printed on your doorstep.

shinpai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>heart</kanji> gets <kanji>parcelled out</kanji>, a scrap of it pinned to every bad thing that might happen. Carry it stretched that thin and you <vocabulary>worry</vocabulary>.

shinsetsu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>parent</kanji> who <kanji>cuts</kanji> the carrots on your plate into small, easy pieces is being <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary>. Treat it as a な adjective and slip な in before the noun it describes.

shinu.meaning_mnemonic: Everything that was keeping you going, heartbeat, breath, the warmth in your hands, switches off one part at a time and does not come back. That final shutdown is what it means to <vocabulary>die</vocabulary>.

shio.meaning_mnemonic: One shake of the white grit makes hot chips worth eating. The same pinch stings like fire in a small cut, because it is <vocabulary>salt</vocabulary>.
shio.reading_mnemonic: Sho the gull cracks white crystals off the <reading>seashore</reading> rocks with her beak. Each crunch sounds like <reading>しお</reading>, and every flake is pure <vocabulary>salt</vocabulary>.

shiro-color.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>white</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>white</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning carries straight across with nothing added.
shiro-color.reading_mnemonic: Down on the riverbank a rower grips the oars so hard that her knuckles go bloodless <vocabulary>white</vocabulary>. Watch <reading>she rows</reading>, and on every stroke she grunts <reading>しろ</reading>.

shiroi.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the <kanji>white</kanji> kanji you already know, so the <vocabulary>white</vocabulary> word means exactly that and no more. The い on the end is the adjective ending, letting the word describe a noun directly.
shiroi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 白 is read 「しろ」 from the word 白, so once you add an い it becomes <reading>しろい</reading>, the describing word for <vocabulary>white</vocabulary>.

shiru.meaning_mnemonic: Once a fact is stuck to you firmly enough that you can produce it the second someone asks, it is yours. Carrying it around like that, always within reach, is what it means to <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> it.
shiru.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a <reading>shrew</reading> always taps the one vending-machine button that still works. It squeaks 「<reading>しる</reading>」 at the gaping hiker, and having a fact locked down and ready like that is what it means to <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> it.

shita-v.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the <kanji>down</kanji> kanji you have met, used on its own as the word <vocabulary>down</vocabulary>.
shita-v.reading_mnemonic: The fastest thing at Sei's school is the cheetah hiding <vocabulary>down</vocabulary> under the bleachers, belly flat to the concrete. Nobody checks that low, so it never gets tagged: <reading>cheetah</reading>, <reading>した</reading>.

shitsumon-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Walk up to the shouting gate at the school and throw its own <kanji>question</kanji> straight back through the bars at it. Flinging a question at something to force it to talk is what it is <vocabulary>to ask a question</vocabulary>.

shitsumon.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the gate won't open until you answer the <kanji>question</kanji> shouted through its bars. Take that same demand for an answer indoors, hand raised, and you are asking a <vocabulary>question</vocabulary>.

shitsurei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You let a small <kanji>fault</kanji> creep into the <kanji>bow</kanji> you owe the room, then slip toward the door. Naming that little rudeness out loud before you go is how you <vocabulary>excuse yourself</vocabulary>.

shizuka.meaning_mnemonic: Deep in the school library at exam time, forty students hold so still you can hear the wall clock two rooms away. That held breath, not one creaking chair in it, is <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>.
shizuka.reading_mnemonic: The students call the library's silence-warden <reading>She's-a-cop</reading> because she books you for breathing too loud. One look from her and the whole room drops <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>, and that hush is <reading>しずか</reading>.

tsutaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>walk along</kanji> a message, carrying it down a line of people one hand to the next, until it reaches the far end. Passing something all the way down the line is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>.
tsutaeru.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>two-tailer</reading> lizard courier sprints between houses, flicking one tail per word so the next house gets the message. A tail-flicked relay like that is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>, and its name is 「<reading>つたえる</reading>」.

tsuyoi.meaning_mnemonic: At the school sports day, one first-year on the tug-of-war rope drags the entire opposing team over the line by herself. Being able to move people who refuse to move is <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>.
tsuyoi.reading_mnemonic: A swamped rowboat slides off down the river until Sue wades in and drags it up the bank alone, the ferryman shouting <reading>'Sue, oi'</reading> after her. Hauling a full boat against the current is <reading>つよい</reading>, plain <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>.

tsuzuki.meaning_mnemonic: The stretch where something that <kanji>continues</kanji> picks up again, right after it looked finished, is its <vocabulary>continuation</vocabulary>.
tsuzuki.reading_mnemonic: Sue the zookeeper never lets a tour end. She jangles her <reading>zoo key</reading>, and 「<reading>つづき</reading>」 unlocks one more gate into the <vocabulary>continuation</vocabulary>.

uchi.meaning_mnemonic: Trip over the cat, howl <reading>ouch</reading>, and the one place nobody outside your circle hears you do it is <reading>うち</reading>, your <vocabulary>home</vocabulary> and everyone inside it.

ue.meaning_mnemonic: Standing by itself, the <kanji>up</kanji> kanji is just the <vocabulary>up</vocabulary> word, nothing added.
ue.reading_mnemonic: A monkey named Louie has stranded his chocolate bar on top of the summit vending machine and cannot reach it. He just points <vocabulary>up</vocabulary> and wails his own name: <reading>Louie</reading>, <reading>うえ</reading>.

ugokasu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>move</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> are the same character, meaning unchanged. The かす ending makes it the transitive one: you are the one shoving something else into motion.
ugokasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this reading of 動 from 動く, so when you are the one making something else move, <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> it, the word is <reading>うごかす</reading>.

ugoku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>move</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> are the same character, so the meaning carries over. The trailing kana mark the intransitive one: the thing shifts on its own, with nobody pushing it.
ugoku.reading_mnemonic: Sei leans on a stalled merry-go-round, mutters <reading>you go, cuckoo</reading>, and it lurches into a slow spin on its own, 「<reading>うごく</reading>」, that first shift from dead still being what it means to <vocabulary>move</vocabulary>.

umareru.meaning_mnemonic: A brand-new <kanji>life</kanji> that was nowhere a minute ago and is suddenly here, breathing on its own. That sudden arrival is what it means to <vocabulary>be born</vocabulary>.
umareru.reading_mnemonic: A stray <reading>mare</reading> wanders onto the school sports field at dawn and drops her foal in the wet grass with no fuss at all. Watching it stagger upright is watching something <vocabulary>be born</vocabulary>, and she nickers a low 「<reading>うまれる</reading>」 over it.

umi.meaning_mnemonic: The one thing wide enough that you cannot see the far side, deep enough that nothing you drop comes back, and salty enough to sting a cut is the <vocabulary>sea</vocabulary>.
umi.reading_mnemonic: A sailor steps off the last dock, sees nothing but water clear to the horizon, thumps his chest and booms 「<reading>うみ</reading>」, like <reading>ooh, me</reading>. All that flat endless salt water in front of him is the <vocabulary>sea</vocabulary>.

unten-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Give the wheels that only <kanji>revolve</kanji> some real road to bite, and the spin finally <kanji>carries</kanji> the whole car forward. Sitting up front making that happen is what it means <vocabulary>to drive</vocabulary>.

ureshii.meaning_mnemonic: A dog hears the leash come off its hook and understands a walk is coming. The whole body wags at once, and that full-body wag is <vocabulary>happy / glad</vocabulary>.
ureshii.reading_mnemonic: Reiko finds one last scoop of <reading>relish</reading> in the jar and does a little hop. Hear <reading>うれしい</reading> as that relish-hop and you have <vocabulary>happy / glad</vocabulary>.

uru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sell</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
uru.reading_mnemonic: A snail runs a little stall on the mossy shrine steps and passes trinkets to the cats one at a time. Every sale leaves a shiny <reading>ooze</reading> trail on the stone, so <reading>うる</reading> means <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary>.

ushiro.meaning_mnemonic: This word is just the <kanji>behind</kanji> kanji you already know, so <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> is exactly what it means.
ushiro.reading_mnemonic: A duck on the riverbank rowed so hard she left the whole regatta <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> her. Watch her wake and you still hear it: <reading>she rowed</reading>, <reading>うしろ</reading>.

uta.meaning_mnemonic: Words turn into a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> the moment a tune picks them up and makes them rise and fall instead of lying flat.
uta.reading_mnemonic: You already met this reading in 歌う, so a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> is just <reading>うた</reading> again.

utau.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> sits silent on the page until a voice lifts it into the air. Pushing it out of your mouth like that is what it means to <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.
utau.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn a cat squeezes inside the shrine's great bell and belts a long note that ends on a proud <reading>you-ta-daa</reading>. The bell booms it back doubled, and that racket is the cat's idea of how to 「<reading>うたう</reading>」 and <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.

wakai.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine, Grandma Kane swears she is still <vocabulary>young</vocabulary> as she chases the cats up the mossy steps two at a time. The い on the end is the marker that makes it an adjective, free to sit before any noun.
wakai.reading_mnemonic: A wacky teenager grinds their skateboard down the school's echoing hallway, shouting that only the <vocabulary>young</vocabulary> would try a stunt this <reading>wacky</reading>. The boast stuck, and now everyone says <reading>わかい</reading>.

wakaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>understand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> word are the same character, so the meaning carries straight over. The kana tacked on the end makes it a verb that just happens on its own.
wakaru.reading_mnemonic: A fisher on the riverbank stares at a tangled line until, all at once, the whole knot resolves in her head and she blurts 「<reading>わかる</reading>」. The cry lands right on <reading>wah-kah-roo</reading>, the sound of a thing you finally <vocabulary>understand</vocabulary>.

warau.meaning_mnemonic: Your mouth pulls wide, your cheeks bunch up under your eyes, and air comes out of you in short barks you cannot hold back. That whole helpless reaction is what it means to <vocabulary>laugh / smile</vocabulary>.
warau.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>walrus</reading> hauls out on the riverbank, flops flat into the mud, and lies there with both flippers up, hugely pleased with itself. You take one look and <vocabulary>laugh / smile</vocabulary>, and its wet, satisfied rumble comes out as 「<reading>わらう</reading>」.

warui.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever noun you set this in front of, it drags the thing down. The い hanging off the end makes it an adjective, and the verdict it lands on is <vocabulary>bad</vocabulary>.
warui.reading_mnemonic: Every time the puppy Rooey chews through another shoe, his owner throws up her hands and groans <reading>wah, Rooey</reading>. That groan is 「<reading>わるい</reading>」, and it means the dog has been <vocabulary>bad</vocabulary>.

wasureru.meaning_mnemonic: You set your keys down somewhere so ordinary your brain never files it, and an hour later that spot is a blank. Letting a thing fall clean out of your head is to <vocabulary>forget</vocabulary> it.
wasureru.reading_mnemonic: Koichi swore he <reading>was surely</reading> saving you the last onigiri, then sold it to the next customer, the promise gone from his head. That clean drop out of mind is to <vocabulary>forget</vocabulary>, and its sound is <reading>わすれる</reading>.

watar.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ford</kanji> the shallow river stepping stone by stepping stone until you reach the far bank. Getting all the way to the other side is what it means to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.
watar.reading_mnemonic: Each step the heron takes through the <reading>water</reading> makes a slow suck and slap, 「<reading>わたる</reading>」, as it works toward the other side. That patient wade is the bird choosing to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.

watashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>private</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>I / me</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
watashi.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hoarder snatches the last piece of sushi and snaps <reading>わたし</reading>, which sounds just like <reading>what a sushi</reading>, because only <vocabulary>me</vocabulary> gets to eat it.

watashitachi.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>private</kanji> stash belongs to one person, but stand a whole row of them side by side and that row becomes <vocabulary>we</vocabulary>.
watashitachi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 私 reads わたし, so adding たち turns <vocabulary>we</vocabulary> into <reading>わたしたち</reading>.

watasu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ferry</kanji> the parcel across the last stretch of counter. Passing it into the customer's open hands is to <vocabulary>hand it over</vocabulary>.
watasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 渡 from 渡る, where it means getting across, so passing a thing all the way into another hand, <vocabulary>to hand over</vocabulary>, is <reading>わたす</reading>.

yakkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: The one <kanji>office</kanji> licensed to weigh out <kanji>medicine</kanji> brewed from bitter grass is a <vocabulary>pharmacy</vocabulary>.

yakusoku.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>promise / appointment</vocabulary> is a <kanji>bundle</kanji> of your own future hours. You tie it shut and hand it to someone else to hold.

yama-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary> word are the same character start to finish, so you already know everything it means.
yama-v.reading_mnemonic: At the petting-zoo hill a stubborn llama plants its feet halfway up and brays 「<reading>やま</reading>」 at the summit, a sound like <reading>llama</reading> itself. The big rock it flatly refuses to climb is a <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary>.

yasai.meaning_mnemonic: Green things that come up on their own out on the untended <kanji>plains</kanji>, with no farmer and no fence, still get gathered up and eaten as <vocabulary>vegetables</vocabulary>.

yasashii.meaning_mnemonic: Today's test at the school is a single question asking whether the sky is above you or below you. Sei circles 'above' without sitting down, because a test that answers itself is <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.
yasashii.reading_mnemonic: A new kid at the school meets every hard question from the teacher with a shrug and a mellow <reading>yeah, sushi</reading>. Nothing rattles him, so his whole week feels <reading>やさしい</reading>, which is to say <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.

yasui-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cheap</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so they mean the same thing. That final い is what turns it into an adjective, a marker every い adjective shares.
yasui-adj.reading_mnemonic: A farmer loads his cart with <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary> bruised apples, so pleased with the price that he calls his pig over with a cheerful <reading>“ya, sooey!”</reading>, which is just <reading>やすい</reading>.

yasumu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>rest</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to rest</vocabulary> word are the same character carrying the same meaning. The kana on the tail is only there so you can conjugate it like a verb.
yasumu.reading_mnemonic: Halfway through his shift, Koichi yawns so hard the till blurs, and he answers a customer with a dozy <reading>'yes, mum'</reading>. He shuts the register and decides to <vocabulary>rest</vocabulary> for what is left of the day, yawning 「<reading>やすむ</reading>」.

yattsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
yattsu.reading_mnemonic: A toy <reading>yacht</reading> capsizes on the riverbank and spills <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> into the current. The kid wading after it yells <reading>やっつ</reading> as they float away.

yobu.meaning_mnemonic: Shout a name across the room and the person turns; say it warmly with a date attached and they show up to dinner. Both are one verb: to <vocabulary>call or invite</vocabulary> someone.
yobu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi leans out the konbini door and shouts <reading>yo, boo</reading> at every regular he spots on the street. To <reading>よぶ</reading> is to <vocabulary>call someone over</vocabulary> until they come in.

yoi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the plain word for good pulling on a stiff, pressed suit. The い ending still makes it an adjective, but that starch is what turns it into <vocabulary>good (formal)</vocabulary>, the version for letters and speeches.
yoi.reading_mnemonic: A ship's lookout leans from the crow's nest and calls a long <reading>yo-eee</reading> each time the water ahead runs clear. That all-clear cry is 「<reading>よい</reading>」, the formal word for conditions that are <vocabulary>good (formal)</vocabulary>.

yokka.meaning_mnemonic: Pacing off all <kanji>four</kanji> walls of that doorless room already burns a whole <kanji>day</kanji>. Four walls at a day apiece add up to <vocabulary>four days</vocabulary>.

yoku.meaning_mnemonic: The old ox at the riverbank has worn its <reading>yoke</reading> so <reading>よく</reading>, day after day, that it now ploughs a straight furrow <vocabulary>well</vocabulary> without a hand on the reins.

yomu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to read</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries straight over.
yomu.reading_mnemonic: A cow sits by the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail with the manual open. It works down the page going <reading>you moo</reading> at each line, because <reading>よむ</reading> is the cow's one skill, <vocabulary>to read</vocabulary>.

yon-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji is the <vocabulary>four</vocabulary> word — nothing added, nothing changed to get here.
yon-v.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker counts his water bottles. His huge <reading>yawn</reading> comes out sounding just like <reading>よん</reading> — he's short exactly <vocabulary>four</vocabulary>.
yon-v.description: Native speakers use this reading rather than the kanji's other reading, because that other reading sounds identical to the word for death and is avoided when counting aloud, especially in hospitals and elevators.

yoru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school gates lock shut the moment <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls, leaving the sports field dark and silent.
yoru.reading_mnemonic: A ghost at the riverbank moans 「<reading>よる</reading>」, which sounds just like calling <reading>your</reading> name, right as <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls.

yotei.meaning_mnemonic: A time you <kanji>fix</kanji> in place <kanji>beforehand</kanji> so the day cannot drift is a <vocabulary>plan / schedule</vocabulary>.

yottsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary> word share the same number, but the added つ turns a bare digit into four items you can point at and count.
yottsu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a collector proudly shows off four half-sunk <reading>yachts</reading>, insisting that's exactly why everyone says <reading>よっつ</reading> when they mean <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary>.

youji.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> you have to leave the house and settle face to face is an <vocabulary>errand</vocabulary>.

youka.meaning_mnemonic: Flip the calendar past <kanji>eight</kanji> pages, each one a <kanji>day</kanji>, and you have flipped through <vocabulary>eight days</vocabulary>.

yowai.meaning_mnemonic: You rest one elbow on the wire shelf by the konbini door and the whole rack folds to the floor, onigiri and all. A thing that gives out the moment anything leans on it is <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary>.
yowai.reading_mnemonic: A shrine kitten takes a run at the bottom mossy step, slides back down on its nose, and gives up. Grandma Kane watches and mutters <reading>'yo, why'</reading> bother, since a cat that <reading>よわい</reading> is exactly what <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary> looks like.

yoyaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You lock in a <kanji>promise</kanji>, made well <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, that one seat stays empty for you and nobody else. Getting that promise on the books is how you <vocabulary>reserve</vocabulary> it.

yuki.meaning_mnemonic: Rain that dawdled on the way down until it froze arrives as soft white clumps on your collar. That heaped, silent pile is <vocabulary>snow</vocabulary>.
yuki.reading_mnemonic: A kid trudges down the mountain trail with both boots packed full of half-melted <vocabulary>snow</vocabulary>. Every squelching step makes her groan 「<reading>ゆき</reading>」, and she is right, because that is genuinely <reading>yucky</reading>.

yukkuri.meaning_mnemonic: You wave Ree back from the beeping till with a calm <reading>ゆっくり</reading>. It is <reading>'you cook, Ree'</reading> at any pace, so the onigiri warms <vocabulary>slowly / leisurely</vocabulary>.

yume.meaning_mnemonic: The film that runs behind your eyes while you sleep, so real you talk back to it, then gone the instant the alarm goes, is a <vocabulary>dream</vocabulary>.
yume.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane bends over the sleeping cats on the shrine steps and whispers 「<reading>ゆめ</reading>」. <reading>You may</reading> fly, you may be rich, she means, but only until dawn, because none of it is real, it is just a <vocabulary>dream</vocabulary>.

yuubinkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>facility</kanji> that handles <kanji>mail</kanji> and refuses to handle anything else is a <vocabulary>post office</vocabulary>.

yuugata.meaning_mnemonic: Every person on the street turns to face the same <kanji>direction</kanji> as the light fades, and that turning hour is <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary>.

yuumei.meaning_mnemonic: Even with your face hidden, a <kanji>name</kanji> that this many strangers already <kanji>have</kanji> in their heads makes you <vocabulary>famous</vocabulary>. It takes な before the noun it describes.

zasshi.meaning_mnemonic: Bind a fat stack of <kanji>miscellaneous</kanji> articles into a single glossy <kanji>document</kanji> and you have printed a <vocabulary>magazine</vocabulary>.

zenbu.meaning_mnemonic: Pull together every single <kanji>section</kanji> of a thing, skip none, and what is left in your hands is the <vocabulary>whole</vocabulary> of it.

zenzen.meaning_mnemonic: You hunt every shelf at Koichi's konbini for any <kanji>sort of thing</kanji> that could count as breakfast. There is nothing like it in the whole shop, <vocabulary>(not) at all</vocabulary>.

zero.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's team loses eleven to nothing, and the scoreboard just flashes the English word for it: <vocabulary>zero</vocabulary>.

shi-city.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>city</kanji> kanji standing on its own is the whole word, so this <vocabulary>city</vocabulary> means exactly what the kanji does.

ooi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>many</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>many</vocabulary> word are the same character. The い hooked on the end marks it as an adjective, a habit every い adjective keeps.
ooi.reading_mnemonic: The crowd packed onto the school sports field is so <vocabulary>many</vocabulary> that when they all shout <reading>oi</reading> at once, that <reading>おおい</reading> wall of sound rattles the windows.
